catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alejandro-her:
Alejandro Herculano de Carvalho e Araújo was a Portuguese historian and writer, born at Lisbon in March 1810 and dead near Santarém in September 1877. His liberal principles forced him into exile under Dom Miguel, and he spent 1828 in Paris and 1830 and 1831 in England. Returning home in 1832, he embraced the romantic doctrines Almeida Garrett preached in Portugal and turned to poetry, journalism, and the historical novel.

His Monasticon, with Eurico the Presbyter in 1844 and its sequel The Monk of Cister in 1848, naturalized the historical novel in Portuguese. His Bobo and Legends and Narratives of 1851 gave modern form to old legends. His History of Portugal in four volumes, covering events to the end of the thirteenth century, belongs to 1846 to 1853. His history of the Inquisition in Portugal appeared in 1854 to 1855. As a member of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences he published documents from the national archives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-de-ar:
Brazilian missionary Antonio de Araujo, born in the Azores at St. Michael's and dead in 1632, spent nine years as superior of the missions of Brazil after joining the Society of Jesus at Bahia. His chief legacy was a catechism, a book of Christian teaching in question and answer form, written in the native language of Brazil. Begun by others, the work was greatly enlarged by Araujo and published at Lisbon under his name.

Southwell, quoted in the article, judged it without a superior in the art of catechism writing, and it was later turned into another native American tongue. The entry is brief, yet it captures a missionary method that prized clear teaching in people's own language over preaching in Portuguese alone. For readers tracing early Brazilian missions, Araujo stands for patient work of translation and instruction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-espej:
Spanish explorer Antonio de Espejo was born at Cordova by his own account, with birth and death dates unknown. He is known for one notable trek into New Mexico and Arizona in 1582 and 1583. Earlier, Coronado's great expedition of 1540 had crossed Pueblo country along the Rio Grande toward Quivira. Two Franciscans left behind had died, one murdered, the first missionary martyred in the United States. Forty years later three more Franciscans set out for the Tigua near present Bernalillo, and rumours of their deaths reached Mexico.

Finding the authorities slow to act, Espejo, a wealthy mining owner, paid for and led a search party north. The article follows that rescue mission through country already touched by Coronado and the friars, and notes that Espejo's later plan for a colonizing expedition failed through the viceroy's jealousy. It is a story of private enterprise filling a gap left by officials.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cristobal-de-:
A biographical entry presents Cristobal de Castillejo, a Spanish poet born at Ciudad Rodrigo in 1491 and dead at Vienna in 1556. From fifteen he served the Infante Ferdinand, brother of Charles V, living many years in Austria as his secretary. Late in life he took orders and retired to a monastery near Vienna.

Castillejo championed the old school of Spanish verse against the Italian measures introduced by Boscan and Garcilasso de la Vega. He argued that native metres could express every sentiment, using the new forms only to mock their champions. Praised for purity, grace, fluency, and humour, he wrote satires so bold that the Inquisition barred his poems until expurgated. His works divide into love, conversation and pastime, and moral and religious verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-: This 1913 reference piece on Francisco de Araújo — the Dominican theologian. William Noon notes his famous works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the seventeenth century. A friar among the schoolmen. His 1635 works are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ghirlandajo: A 1913 entry on Ghirlandaio — the Florentine master. Louis Gillet honors his famous frescoes. His brush crowned the Medici chapels. The city prized the gifted hand. The teacher of the young Michelangelo. His 1494 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portoviejo: Portoviejo, the Manabí city of Ecuador's coast, became a diocese. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history as of 1913. The faith in the land of the ceibo trees: its modest cathedral serves all of coastal Manabí province faithfully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-toribio-al: St. Toribio Mogrovejo was the archbishop of Lima. This entry traces his visitations, his Indians, and his fame. The apostle of the Peruvian church: his great see crowned Lima in the 1580s' Peru in the city of the kings in America.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ConnallyJohnBJr:
Governor John Connally of Texas was riding in the same car as President John F. Kennedy when Kennedy was shot in Dallas. A medical article by Nichols, an emeritus professor of pathology at the University of Kansas Medical Center, examines the wounds Connally himself suffered that day. The piece is presented as the author's own viewpoint.

Nichols writes as a pathologist, working through what Connally's injuries show about the bullets that struck him. Wound paths and damage matter here because Connally's injuries have long been central to arguments about how many shots were fired. The article gives readers a medical reading of wounds usually discussed in political terms.
podcast-joerogan-4Uk0_1yqdJo:
Parapsychologist Dean Radin joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2513. Radin has run lab studies on psi for decades, testing claims such as mind-to-mind links and knowing events before they happen. His work sits far outside the science mainstream, which is why Rogan booked him.

Radin explains his best-known experiments and the statistics he says point to real effects. Rogan asks the hard questions a skeptic would ask, about fraud, luck, and failed repeats of the tests. The episode lets listeners judge a careful case for strange powers, made by the man who has spent his career trying to prove them.
podcast-joerogan-nvcXs0RXWJo:
Toad venom and DMT drive this Joe Rogan Experience segment on the strongest psychedelic experiences known. The focus is 5-MeO-DMT, a compound found in the venom of a desert toad. Smoked, it hits within seconds and can erase any sense of self.

Rogan and his guest describe what the trip feels like and why people seek it out. They compare it with standard DMT and talk about fear, surrender, and life-changing aftereffects. Risks get airtime too, since the dose is hard to control. It is a frank talk about an intense drug, told by people who respect its power.
the-cruise-of-the-alabama-and-the-sumter: Printed in New York in 1864 by Geo. W. Carleton, this account of the cruise of the steamers Sumter and Alabama, in two volumes bound as one, is drawn from the journals and papers of Commander R. Semmes and other officers. A London advertisement explains that a narrative form was sometimes used. The aim was to keep as close to Semmes's own words as possible, with help from officers Lieutenant R. F. Armstrong and Master's Mate G. Townley Fullam. Only the title pages and that advertisement are present here.
